opus-5.5.text:
I think "world model" has become one of those terms everyone uses but almost no one defines the same way. So let me give you my own understanding rather than pretend there's a consensus.

At the most basic level, a world model is an internal representation that lets an agent predict how the world will evolve, especially in response to its own actions. If I push this cup, it slides; if I let go, it falls. Humans and animals do this constantly and mostly unconsciously. We aren't just recognizing what's in front of us; we're running a little simulation of what happens next. That predictive, action-conditioned piece is, to me, the core.

Where I think people get confused is in equating a world model with a video generator. Generating beautiful, realistic pixels is impressive, but realism alone doesn't mean the system understands anything. You can produce a plausible-looking video of a ball bouncing without having any consistent notion of objects, physics, or cause and effect. A real world model should capture the underlying structure: persistence, geometry, dynamics, what's controllable and what isn't. Whether you render that into pixels is almost secondary. In some sense, the rendering is a decoder; the model is what sits underneath.

This connects to something I care about a lot, which is visual representation learning. For a long time, the field treated vision as a recognition problem: label the image, detect the object. Then language models took off, and vision was often treated as a front end that converts images into tokens for the LLM to reason over. I think that's backwards in an important way. Language is a very compressed, human-curated description of the world. It's extremely useful, but it's not the world itself. A lot of what we know about physical reality, like spatial reasoning, intuitive physics, and how things move and interact, was never written down. It has to be learned from sensory experience, and vision is the richest channel we have for that.

So when I think about world models, I think about systems that learn from visual and embodied experience to build grounded, predictive representations of space and time. Not just "what is this," but "where is it, how does it relate to everything else, and what happens if I act." Spatial intelligence is a big part of that, and I'd argue current multimodal models are still surprisingly weak there, even when they sound fluent.

One more thing I'd add: a world model isn't valuable for its own sake. Its value is in planning and decision-making. If you have a good model of the world, you can imagine consequences before acting, try things in your head, and generalize to situations you've never seen. That's what makes it a step toward more general intelligence, rather than just a better content-generation tool.

So my short answer: a world model is a learned, grounded, predictive model of how the world works, built largely from perception, that an agent can use to imagine and plan. We're still pretty early in figuring out how to build one properly, and honestly, that's what makes it exciting.

r001.rationale: It describes a world model as capturing spatial structure, geometry, persistence, and controllability, beyond predicting how the world evolves over time.

r002.rationale: It describes action-conditioned prediction of how the world evolves, but does not clearly define the model as a transition function conditioned on the current state and an applied action.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and honestly the term has become a bit of a Rorschach test — everyone sees something different in it. So let me try to give you my own working definition rather than a textbook one.

At the most basic level, a world model is a system that has an internal representation of how the world works, so that it can predict what happens next, and reason about what would happen if it took some action. The key word there is "predict." Not just recognize, not just describe, but anticipate. If I push this cup off the table, it falls. If I walk around that corner, the room continues to exist. If I don't see the car for two seconds because a truck passed in front of it, the car is still there and has moved roughly where I'd expect. Those are all little predictions, and humans make thousands of them every second without noticing.

Now, where I think a lot of confusion comes from is that people conflate "world model" with "video generation model." The two are related, but they're not the same thing. A video generator predicts pixels. A world model predicts *states* — the underlying structure that gives rise to the pixels. You can have a model that produces beautiful, coherent-looking video and still has no real understanding that objects persist, that there's a consistent 3D space, that gravity points down. It's learned the statistics of video, not the structure of the world. Conversely, you could imagine a world model that's quite bad at rendering pretty frames but very good at knowing where things are and what they'll do.

So in my mind there are a few ingredients that matter. One is spatial understanding — a sense of 3D, of geometry, of where things are relative to each other, not just in the image plane. Language models are actually remarkably weak here, and I think that's one of the biggest blind spots in the current paradigm. Two is temporal consistency and dynamics — knowing how things evolve and what causes what. Three is counterfactual reasoning — being able to imagine "what if I did X instead of Y." That last one is what makes it useful for planning, for agents, for robotics.

I'd also say it's worth separating the representation from the generation. A lot of my own recent thinking is that we've been over-indexing on generation as the objective. Generating every pixel is an extremely expensive way to learn about the world, and much of that effort goes into details that don't matter for understanding — the exact texture of the wall, the lighting noise. The interesting question is whether you can learn a compressed, predictive representation where the model only has to get the important things right. That's closer to how I think about what a "good" world model should be.

And then there's the question of embodiment. I don't think you get a complete world model purely from passive observation. Humans learn a huge amount from interaction — reaching, failing, trying again. So I suspect the models that end up really deserving the name will be ones that are trained in a loop with action, not just on scraped video.

So if I had to compress it into one sentence: a world model is a learned, predictive, ideally spatial and causal representation of the environment that lets a system reason about what it hasn't observed yet. Whether any current system fully meets that bar — I'd say we're clearly making progress, but we're still early, and we should be a bit careful about using the label too loosely.

r001.rationale: It describes predicting what happens next and reasoning about what would happen under an action, including counterfactuals, so the model is not limited to temporal prediction.

r002.rationale: It says a world model predicts what would happen if the system took an action, and illustrates this with pushing a cup in its current setting and predicting that it falls—communicating an action-conditioned prediction from the environment.

astra-6.text:
I think “world model” is a fairly broad term, so I would start with what we want the model to do. It should learn something about how the world works from observations, and use that understanding to predict what might happen next—especially what might happen if you take a particular action.

For example, if I push a cup toward the edge of a table, can the model anticipate that it might fall? That requires more than recognizing a cup and a table. It requires some understanding of their relationship, how things move, and how an action changes the situation.

Video prediction is one way to approach this, because video gives us observations of a changing world. But generating a plausible-looking video doesn’t necessarily mean you have learned the underlying dynamics well enough to plan or act. A model can produce something visually convincing and still get the consequences of an action wrong.

So, for me, the key question is whether the model has learned a representation that supports prediction and decision-making. That representation doesn’t necessarily need to reconstruct every pixel. It needs to capture the aspects of the world that matter for what you’re trying to do. That’s what makes a world model useful: you can use it to consider possibilities before actually taking an action.

r001.rationale: The response says video prediction alone is insufficient and emphasizes a representation for prediction and decision-making, including considering possibilities before acting.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting what happens next from observations, especially what happens when a particular action is taken, and illustrates how pushing a cup changes the situation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “world model” is a pretty broad term, so I would start by asking: what aspects of the world are we trying to model, and for what purpose? At a basic level, it’s an internal model that lets an intelligent system understand how its environment works and anticipate what might happen next.

For example, if I push a cup toward the edge of a table, I can imagine it falling without actually doing it. That prediction involves more than recognizing a cup. It involves understanding space, physical interactions, and the consequences of an action.

In AI, predicting future video frames is one way to approach this. But I wouldn’t equate a world model with a video generator. You can generate something visually plausible without necessarily understanding how actions change the environment. To me, the more interesting question is whether the model captures enough of that underlying structure to support decisions: if I do this, what happens, and what should I do next?

It also doesn’t need to simulate every detail. A useful world model should capture the details that matter for the task. So I see it less as a perfect replica of reality and more as a representation that enables prediction, interaction, and planning.

r001.rationale: The response says a world model is broader than predicting future video frames and describes it as supporting interaction, decisions, and planning.

r002.rationale: The response discusses predicting what happens after an action, but does not clearly define the model as a transition function conditioned on both the current environment state and the applied action.
